value.overview: The Great Egret (Ardea alba) is a large, elegant heron found on wetlands across much of the world. It is recognized by its entirely white plumage, long neck and legs, yellow bill, and slow, deliberate movements while hunting. The species uses both freshwater and coastal habitats and often shares nesting colonies with other herons and egrets. In Costa Rica, it is a familiar wetland bird and may be seen in both lowland and coastal areas.
value.classification: The Great Egret belongs to the heron family, Ardeidae, in the order Pelecaniformes. It is also called the Great White Egret or Great White Heron in some regions.
value.identification: A Great Egret is a tall, slender, completely white wading bird with a long, S-shaped neck, long black legs, and a long, pointed yellow bill. It is larger and more slender than a Snowy Egret, which has a black bill and yellow feet. During the breeding season, adults develop long ornamental plumes on the back, and the facial skin near the bill may become greenish. In flight, the neck is folded and the broad wings beat slowly.
value.rangeHabitat: The species has a broad distribution in the Americas, Europe, Africa, Asia, and Australasia. It occupies marshes, swamps, ponds, lakeshores, flooded fields, rice fields, river edges, mangroves, estuaries, mudflats, and sheltered coastal waters. In Costa Rica, Great Egrets occur widely in suitable lowland wetlands, along rivers, around lakes and ponds, in mangroves, and on coastal mudflats. They are recorded on both the Pacific and Caribbean sides of the country, as well as inland.
value.migrationStatus: Great Egrets in Costa Rica include resident birds and seasonal visitors. Some local populations remain year-round, while additional individuals migrate south from North America and occur mainly during the nonbreeding season or passage periods. Numbers can therefore increase seasonally, especially in wetlands and coastal areas.
value.breeding: Great Egrets usually breed in colonies, often with other herons, egrets, and ibises. Nests are built on trees, shrubs, or vegetation near water and are made from sticks. Both adults help incubate the eggs and feed the young. Several young may hatch, but competition among nestlings can be intense when food is scarce. Great Egrets breed in parts of their tropical range, including suitable wetland areas of Costa Rica, although timing varies with local rainfall and water conditions.
value.dietFeeding: The diet consists mainly of fish, frogs, aquatic insects, crustaceans, and other small aquatic animals. Great Egrets may also take snakes, lizards, small mammals, and occasionally young birds. They commonly hunt by standing motionless in shallow water or walking slowly while watching for prey. When an opportunity appears, the bird thrusts its bill forward with a rapid stabbing motion. It may also forage in flooded fields, grasslands, and along tidal edges.
value.behavior: Great Egrets are usually solitary while feeding but gather at communal roosts and breeding colonies. They are patient hunters and may remain still for long periods before striking. Birds often fly with slow, powerful wingbeats and the neck folded back. They are active during daylight and may move between wetlands as water levels and prey availability change. Outside the breeding season, they can travel widely and may appear in habitats far from traditional nesting sites.

conservation.populationTrend: The global population trend is uncertain. The species is widespread and remains common in many regions, although local populations may increase or decline depending on wetland condition and protection.
